Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 633 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

Last spring my cousin Dana had to decide whether to take a job offer in Denver or stay in her hometown and finish her nursing degree. She asked her mother first, and her mother said, without pausing, "Stay. Family is here." If Dana had stopped there, she probably would have stayed. Instead she kept asking, and that is a big part of why her final choice turned out well. Seeking more than one opinion helps a person decide better because it exposes blind spots, reveals different kinds of knowledge, and forces the person to understand her own reasons.

The first benefit is that every adviser has a bias, and several advisers cancel each other out. Dana's mother wanted her close because she would miss her. That does not make her advice worthless, but it does mean the advice was partly about the mother's feelings. When Dana asked her older friend Marcus, who had moved away for work years before, he told her that leaving was the best thing he ever did. His view was shaped by his own history too. Neither person was lying. Each was describing the world as they had experienced it. By hearing both, Dana could see where the advice came from and discount it accordingly. One opinion looks like a fact. Two opinions that disagree look like what they really are, perspectives.

The second benefit is that different people know different things. Dana also talked to a nursing instructor, who pointed out something neither her mother nor Marcus had considered. The Denver job was in billing, not patient care, and leaving school without a degree would make it hard to return to clinical work later. Dana had been so excited about the salary that she had not thought about where the job would lead in five years. Her instructor had watched many students make the same jump and knew how it usually ended. That detail was information Dana could not have gotten from people who loved her but did not work in the field. A single adviser, however kind, only holds one slice of what is useful to know.

Third, asking several people makes a person explain the problem more than once, and explaining is a kind of thinking. By the third conversation Dana noticed she kept saying the same thing: she did not actually want to leave her program. She wanted to feel that she was moving forward. Each person asked a slightly different question, and each question pushed her to say what mattered most. Sometimes the greatest value of an outside opinion is not the answer but the question it provokes. When Marcus asked, "What would you regret more?" she realized she would regret abandoning her degree far more than turning down a job.

Of course, collecting opinions has limits. Too many voices can be paralyzing, and a person who asks ten people may just be hunting for someone to say what she already wants to hear. The goal is not to count votes. Dana did not follow the majority; she weighed the reasons behind each view. A good rule is to ask a few people with different backgrounds and then to look at their reasoning instead of their conclusions.

In the end Dana stayed, finished her degree, and later accepted a better position at a hospital in Denver. Her mother was right about waiting, Marcus was right about moving, and the instructor was right about timing. No one person had the whole picture, but together they gave her enough of it to choose with confidence. That is why asking more than one person is not a sign of weak judgment. It is a way of strengthening it, because a decision built on several honest views stands on firmer ground than one built on a single voice.
